title: Blue-enriched white light in the workplace improves self-reported alertness, performance and sleep quality
authors: Viola AU, James LM, Schlangen LJM, Dijk D-J
research_question: To investigate the effects of exposure to blue-enriched white light during daytime workhours in an office setting on self-reported alertness, performance, and sleep quality.

participants.description: 104 white-collar workers (94 included in analysis, mean age 36.4 years, SD 10.2) from a distribution company for electronic parts in northern England (latitude 52 degrees north).
participants.recruitment: All participants gave written informed consent; favorably reviewed by University of Surrey Ethics Committee.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three lighting conditions in an office setting: 1) Baseline (basic white halophosphate lamps, horizontal average illuminance 409.11 lx, irradiance 1.32 to 6.14 µW/cm²). 2) Blue-enriched white light (17 000 K, Philips master TL-D Activiva Active, mean illuminance 310.35 lx, irradiance 2.58 to 6.42 × 1014 µW/cm²). 3) White light (4000 K, Philips master TL-D super 80, mean illuminance 421.07 lx, irradiance 2.4 to 4.49 × 1014 µW/cm²). The 17000K light had more output between 420-480 nm.

measures.construct: Vitality, energy, activity, alertness, concentration, tiredness, trouble thinking

measures.instrument: Past Two Weeks Questionnaire (9-point Likert scale)
Morning Need of Recovery Scale (modified version)

mechanisms: Activation of the melanopsin-based photoreceptive system in intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, which are most sensitive to short wavelengths (approx. 480 nm).
Nonvisual effects of light mediated by projections from retinal ganglion cells to hypothalamus, brain stem, thalamus, and other brain areas involved in sleepiness, attention, and working memory.
Impact on pupil responses, contributing to improved visual comfort.
Enhancement of nocturnal melatonin secretion, leading to improved sleep quality and subsequent daytime alertness/performance.
moderators: Expectation about the effect of light treatments
implementation_implications: Enriching the spectral composition of light sources with short wavelengths can improve waking functioning, visual comfort, and sleep quality in occupational settings.
Blue-enriched white light can be beneficial for normal office hours without abnormal sleep-wake schedules.
Positive effects are unlikely to diminish over time for longer exposures to blue-enriched white light.

tables.description: Effect of light exposure conditions on sleep, as assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI).

Effect of experimental light on mood, eye strain, headaches, mental effort, and sleepiness, as assessed by the Positive and Negative Effect Scale (PANAS), the Eye Strain and Headache Questionnaire, the Mental Effort Rating Scale, and the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS).
key_stats: Positive mood: P=0.005 (Light effect), P=0.03 (Order effect), P<0.0001 (Light × order effect)
Negative mood: P=0.3 (Light effect), P=0.23 (Order effect), P<0.0001 (Light × order effect)

limitations: The cross-over design minimized interindividual differences in expectation, but expectation effects still contributed to order effects and some outcomes.
The study was conducted during winter months, which minimized confounding from natural photoperiod lengthening, but seasonal effects were not entirely ruled out for all variables.
The study was conducted in a specific office setting, limiting generalizability to other architectural styles, seasons, or latitudes.
